Graphs . Let 𝖦 = ( 𝖵 , 𝖤 ) \mathsf{G}=(\mathsf{V},\mathsf{E}) be an undirected graph on n = | 𝖵 | n=|\mathsf{V}| nodes with edges 𝖤 \mathsf{E} . We represent the edges via an adjacency matrix 𝐀 ∈ ℝ n × n \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} where the entry 𝐀 u ​ v \mathbf{A}_{uv} for u , v ∈ 𝖵 u,v\in\mathsf{V} is 1 1 if the edge ( u , v ) ∈ 𝖤 (u,v)\in\mathsf{E} and 0 0 otherwise. Let 𝐃 \mathbf{D} be the diagonal degree matrix with entry 𝐃 v ​ v = d v \mathbf{D}_{vv}=d_{v} equal to the degree of v v . The graph Laplacian is defined as 𝐋 := 𝐃 − 𝐀 \mathbf{L}:=\mathbf{D}-\mathbf{A} and the random walk normalized graph Laplacian is defined as ℒ := 𝐈 − 𝐃 − 𝟏 ​ 𝐀 \mathbf{\mathcal{L}}:=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{D^{-1}A} . We assume that at each node v ∈ 𝖵 v\in\mathsf{V} we are given a c c -dimensional signal (or node feature) 𝐱 v ∈ ℝ c \mathbf{x}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} and group such signals into a matrix 𝐗 ∈ ℝ n × c \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times c} .

GNNs and feature transformations . A feature transformation on a graph 𝖦 \mathsf{G} is a permutation-equivariant map f 𝖦 : ℝ n × c 1 → ℝ n × c 2 f_{\mathsf{G}}:\mathbb{R}^{n\times c_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n\times c_{2}} that transforms the node signals. A GNN 𝚯 \operatorname{GNN}_{\bm{\Theta}} is a (continuous) map parameterized by 𝚯 \bm{\Theta} that takes as input a graph alongside node signals 𝖦 = ( 𝖵 , 𝖤 , 𝐗 ) \mathsf{G}=(\mathsf{V},\mathsf{E},\mathbf{X}) and outputs a transformed signal ( 𝖵 , 𝖤 , 𝐗 ′ ) (\mathsf{V},\mathsf{E},\mathbf{X^{\prime}}) . A GNN on a graph 𝖦 \mathsf{G} is therefore a feature transformation GNN Θ : ℝ n × c 1 → ℝ n × c 2 \operatorname{GNN}_{\Theta}:\mathbb{R}^{n\times c_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n\times c_{2}} . Given a collection of graphs 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , a feature transformation F F on 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is an assignment of every graph 𝖦 ∈ 𝒢 \mathsf{G}\in\mathcal{G} to a feature transformation F G : ℝ n G × c 1 → ℝ n G × c 2 F_{G}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{G}\times c_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n_{G}\times c_{2}} . The set of continuous feature transformations over a collection of graphs in 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is denoted 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝒢 , ℝ c 1 , ℝ c 2 ) \mathcal{C}\left(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{R}^{c_{1}},\mathbb{R}^{c_{2}}\right) .

Cellular sheaves . A cellular sheaf ( Curry, 2014 ) ( ℱ , 𝖦 ) \left(\mathcal{F},\mathsf{G}\right) over an undirected graph 𝖦 = ( 𝖵 , 𝖤 ) \mathsf{G}=\left(\mathsf{V},\mathsf{E}\right) augments 𝖦 \mathsf{G} by attaching to each node v v and edge e e a vector space space called stalks and denoted by ℱ ⁡ ( v ) \mathcal{F}(v) and ℱ ⁡ ( e ) \mathcal{F}(e) , usually the stalks are copies of ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} for some d d . Additionally, every incident node-edge pair v ​ ⊴ ​ e v\trianglelefteq e gets assigned a linear map between stalks called restriction maps and denoted ℱ v ​ ⊴ ​ e : ℱ ⁡ ( v ) → ℱ ⁡ ( e ) \mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(v)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(e) . These matrices act as bundle generalizations of their well-known standard graph counterparts and we recover such matrices when ℱ ⁡ ( v ) ≅ ℝ \mathcal{F}(v)\cong\mathbb{R} and ℱ v ​ ⊴ ​ e ​ v = 1 \mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e}{v}=1 for all v ∈ 𝖵 v\in\mathsf{V} and e ∈ 𝖤 e\in\mathsf{E} .

Vector bundles . When restriction maps are orthogonal, we call the sheaf a vector bundle , a structure analogous to connections on Riemannian manifolds. For this reason, the sheaf Laplacian also takes the name connection Laplacian ( Singer & Wu, 2012 ) . The product ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e T ​ ℱ v ​ ⊴ ​ e \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}^{T}\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e} is then also orthogonal and is denoted 𝐎 u ​ v \mathbf{O}_{uv} referring to the transformation a vector undergoes when moved across a manifold via parallel transport. In this case we denote the node-stalk at v v by ℬ ⁡ ( v ) \mathcal{B}(v) , the bundle-adjacency by 𝐀 ℬ \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{B}} and the bundle Laplacian 𝐋 ℬ \mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{B}} , and its normalized version ℒ ℬ := 𝐈 d ​ n × d ​ n − 𝐃 ℬ − 1 ​ 𝐀 ℬ \mathbf{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathcal{B}}:=\mathbf{I}_{dn\times dn}-\mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{B}} .

3 Bundle Neural Networks

In this section, we derive BuNN from heat diffusion equations over flat vector bundles. We then discuss its relationship to GCN ( Kipf & Welling, 2017 ) and NSD ( Bodnar et al., 2022 ) . We provide algorithmic implementations and additional practical details in the Appendix (Section E ).

ℋ ℬ ​ ( t ) = lim K → ∞ ∑ k = 0 K ( − t ​ ℒ ℬ ) k k ! . \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}(t)=\lim_{K\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{\left(-t\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}}\right)^{k}}{k!}.

Computing the heat kernel is necessary to solve the heat equation. An exact solution can be computed using spectral methods. For small t t , one can instead consider the truncated Taylor expansion centered at 0 0 , which amounts to fixing a K K in the above equation. Bodnar et al. (2022) instead approximates the solution using the Euler discretization of the heat equation with unit time step.

However, all these methods pose a challenge when the bundle structure is learned as in Bodnar et al. (2022) , since the heat kernel has to be recomputed after every gradient update of the bundle structure. This high computational overhead limits the usability of Sheaf Neural Networks in applications.

Flat vector bundles . To address the scalability issues of general sheaves and vector bundles, we consider the special case of flat vector bundles in which every node u u gets assigned an orthogonal map 𝐎 u \mathbf{O}_{u} , and every connection factorizes as 𝐎 v ​ u = 𝐎 v T ​ 𝐎 u \mathbf{O}_{vu}=\mathbf{O}_{v}^{T}\mathbf{O}_{u} . Consequently, the bundle Laplacian factors:

where 𝐎 ∈ ℝ n ​ d × n ​ d \mathbf{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd} is block diagonal with v v -th block being 𝐎 v \mathbf{O}_{v} . We call the matrices 𝐎 \mathbf{O} and 𝐎 T \mathbf{O}^{T} synchronization and desynchronization, respectively. We compare different Laplacians in Figure 2 . This factorization avoids the 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 3 ​ | 𝖤 | ) \mathcal{O}\left(d^{3}|\mathsf{E}|\right) cost of computing the restriction map over each edge. Additionally, Lemma 3.1 shows that it allows to cast the bundle heat equation into a standard graph heat equation. This reduces the computation of the bundle heat kernel to that of the cheaper graph heat kernel, an operator that does not change depending on the bundle and can, therefore, also be pre-computed.

The diffusion time t t in Equation 3 is a hyperparameter determining the scale at which messages are diffused. For the case of small t t , we approximate the heat kernel via its truncated Taylor series of degree K K , and for large t t , we use spectral methods. For simplicity of exposition, the steps above describe an update given a single bundle (i.e., c = d c=d ), meaning that 𝐱 v ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{x}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . In general, we allow multiple bundles and vector field channels (Appendix E ). Note that Equations 1 , 2 , and 3 are linear (or affine), and the non-linearities lie in 4 . Equation 2 may be interpreted as a bundle-aware encoder, while Equation 3 is the message diffusion step guided by the heat kernel.

Without the bundle structure, Equation 3 would converge exponentially fast to constant node representations over the graph (e.g. Theorem 1 1 in Li et al. (2018) ), potentially leading to over-smoothing. This is a limitation of existing diffusion-based GNNs ( Xu et al., 2019a ; Zhao et al., 2021 ) . Accordingly, the bundle is crucial in this formulation to prevent node features from collapsing.

Link to Graph Convolutional Networks . It is possible to derive Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) ( Kipf & Welling, 2017 ) as an approximation of BuNNs operating over a trivial bundle. The approximation exp ⁡ ( − ℒ 𝖦 ) ≈ 𝐈 − ℒ 𝖦 \exp(-\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{G}})\approx\mathbf{I}-\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{G}} gives the update 𝐙 ( l + 1 ) = ( 1 − ℒ 𝖦 ) ​ 𝐇 ( l ) = 𝐀 𝖦 ​ 𝐇 ( l ) \mathbf{Z}^{(l+1)}=(1-\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{G}})\mathbf{H}^{(l)}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathsf{G}}\mathbf{H}^{(l)} recovering the GCN update.

Comparison with Sheaf Neural Networks . Flat vector bundles are a special case of cellular sheaves ( Curry, 2014 ; Bodnar et al., 2022 ) , meaning that our model has close connections to Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) ( Hansen & Gebhart, 2020 ; Bodnar et al., 2022 ; Barbero et al., 2022b ; Barbero et al., 2022a ) . While most SNNs operate on fixed sheaves ( Hansen & Gebhart, 2020 ; Barbero et al., 2022a ; Battiloro et al., 2023 ) , we focus on learning sheaves as in Neural Sheaf Diffusion (NSD) from Bodnar et al. (2022) . BuNNs distinguish themselves from NSD in several ways. First, NSD approximates the heat equation using a time-discretized solution to the heat equation, which results in a standard message passing algorithm. In contrast, the direct use of the heat kernel allows BuNNs to break away from the explicit message-passing paradigm . This is in line with Battiloro et al. (2024) who define convolutions on manifolds using the heat kernel of fixed sheaves. Secondly, the use of flat bundles increases scalability since the bundle maps are computed at the node level. Additionally, flat bundles guarantees path independence , a requirement for the theory on the long time limit of NSD in Bodnar et al. (2022) to hold, often not satisfied for general sheaf constructions such as ones used in NSD. Thirdly, we allow ϕ \phi to be any GNN while NSD restricts ϕ \phi to be an MLP. We found that incorporating the graph structure in ϕ \phi improved the experimental results. The update in Equation 2 is also different to NSD in how the 𝐖 \mathbf{W} and 𝐛 \mathbf{b} are applied, and is necessary to prove our main theoretical result, Theorem 5.3 . Additionally, Bodnar et al. (2022) experiments with general restriction maps as opposed to restricting them to orthogonal maps, and find that in practice orthogonal restrictions perform better, hence we consider orthogonal restriction maps. We provide experimental comparisons to NSDs in the experimental section and show that BuNNs significantly outperform their sheaf counterparts. We provide a summarized comparison between GCNs, SNNs, and BuNNs in Table 1 .

Comparison with other methods . Another paradigm for learning on graphs is using graph transformers (GT), where every nodes communicate to each other through the use of self-attention. When the graph transformer is fully connected, all nodes communicate and therefore GT should not suffer from under-reaching or over-squashing, but might suffer from over-smoothing ( Dovonon et al., 2024 ) . When not fully connected, they might suffer from over-squashing ( Barbero et al., 2024 ) . Other paradigms such as Implicit Graph Neural Networks Fu et al. (2023) are also designed to tackle under-reaching and long-range dependencies while empirically not suffering from over-smoothing.

Appendix E Algorithmic and Implementation details

In this section, we provide more details on the implementation of BuNNs. We start by discussing how to use several vector-field channels when the input dimension is greater than the bundle dimension. We then discuss how to use several bundles at once when a single bundle is insufficient. We then combine both views, namely having several vector-field channels on several bundles at once. Finally, we describe how we compute our bundle maps in the experiments.

Extending to several vector-field channels . When the signal dimension exceeds the bundle dimension, i.e. c > d c>d , we cannot directly apply BuNNs to the input signal. In that case, we first transform the signal into a hidden dimension, a multiple of the bundle dimension, i.e. c = d ​ p c=dp . We reshape the input signal into p p channels of d d -dimensional vector fields, where we apply the diffusion step (Equation 3 ) on each p p channels simultaneously, and we apply the weight matrix 𝐖 ∈ ℝ d ​ p × d ​ p \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{dp\times dp} by first flattening the node signals into d ​ p dp dimensions, then multiplying by 𝐖 \mathbf{W} , and then reshaping it into p p channels of d d dimensional vector fields.

Extending to several bundles . Learning a high dimensional orthogonal matrix O( d d ) becomes expensive since the manifold of orthogonal matrices is d ⁡ ( d − 1 ) 2 \frac{d(d-1)}{2} dimensional. However, we can compute many low-dimensional bundles in parallel. In practice, we found that using several 2 2 -dimensional bundles was enough. Computing b b different 2 2 -dimensional bundles requires only b b -parameters since the manifold O( 2 2 ) is 1 1 -dimensional. We, therefore, also use different ‘bundle channels’ given by an additional hyper-parameter – the number of bundles, which we denote b b . Given an input signal of dimension c = d ​ b c=db , we can decompose the signal into b b bundle channels of dimension d d . We can compute the diffusion step (Equation 3 ) for each bundle in parallel. For the update step (Equation 2 ), we apply the weight matrix 𝐖 ∈ ℝ b ​ d × b ​ d \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{bd\times bd} by first flattening the node signals into b ​ d bd dimensions, then multiplying by 𝐖 \mathbf{W} , and then reshaping it into b b bundle channels of d d dimensional vector fields over b b different bundle structures.
Remark E.1 .

We note that using b b different d d dimensional bundles is equivalent to parameterizing a subset of one b ​ d bd -dimensional structure, consisting of the orthogonal map 𝐎 ∈ O ⁡ ( b ​ d ) ⊂ ℝ b ​ d × b ​ d \mathbf{O}\in O(bd)\subset\mathbb{R}^{bd\times bd} that are block diagonal matrices 𝐎 = ⨁ i = 1 ​ … ​ b 𝐎 i \mathbf{O}=\bigoplus_{i=1\ldots b}\mathbf{O}_{i} , with each 𝐎 i ∈ O ⁡ ( d ) \mathbf{O}_{i}\in O(d) .

Extending to several bundles and vector-field channels . We can combine the above two observations. Given an input signal of dimension c = b ​ d ​ p c=bdp , we can subdivide this into b b different bundle structures of dimension d d and p p channels for each bundle. We diffuse on the appropriate bundle structure and flatten the vector fields into a c × c c\times c vector before applying the learnable parameters.

Computing the bundle maps . In our experiments, we noticed that having several bundles of dimension 2 2 was more efficient than one bundle of large dimensions, while there was no clear performance gain when using higher dimensional bundles. To compute the b b bundle maps 𝐎 v \mathbf{O}_{v} we therefore only need b b rotation angles θ v \theta_{v} , one per bundle. In our experiments, we use Housholder reflections using the python package Obukhov (2021) or direct parameterization. Spectral method . We now describe how to implement a BuNN layer using the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the Laplacian.
